newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open firm on dollar, newspaper item.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open firm on dollar, newspaper item.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Friday ahead of two significant economic releases, aided by a strong dollar and an article on Federal Reserve policy in The Washington Post, analysts said.
The dollar set a fresh high against the mark overnight.

The Washington Post piece by John Berry, "Fed Holding Off On Rate Increases" asserted that "senior Federal Reserve officials appear unlikely to raise short-term interest rates anytime soon as a precaution against a resurgence of inflation triggered by the nation's extremely tight labor markets."
The Washington Post said policymakers are not entirely sure why inflation has remained so low despite a 5.3 percent unemployment rate.

"As a result, they will rasie rates only if there are clear signs the situation is changing for the worse -- and at the moment there are none, according to a number of Fed officials," the article said.

"The market got a little bit of help with the dollar overnight and (from) the (Washington) Post article, too, suggesting no Fed tightening near term," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International.

The market gets two substantive economic reports on Friday. The November international trade figures, due at 0830 EST/1330, are expected to show that the U.S. trade deficit widened in November to $9.8 billion after shrinking 30 percent to $7.99 billion in October.
Slow overseas growth, a strong dollar and brisk U.S. economic growth would be the fundamental factors behind the deficit, economists said.
The trade data will enter into economists' fourth-quarter GDP forecasts. GDP (Gross Domestic Product) data are due on January 31.

The market data on December industrial production at 0915 EST/1415 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters forecasted, on average, that production rose 0.6 percent last month after a 0.9 percent November gain.

The portion of the nation's mines, utilities and factories employed in that production, known as capacity utilization, should be 83.5 percent, economists said, up from 83.3 percent in November but safely below levels that raise fears of production bottlenecks and potential inflation pressures.
Friday's trading session precedes a three-day holiday weekend and will be an abbreviated one in advance of that.
The market will be closed on Monday in honor of the birthday of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., the American civil rights leader.

"The trading session will be active in the morning because both the trade numbers and the industrial production numbers are important," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "The trade number will give us a clearer idea of how strong GDP will be, whether it will be in the middle 3.0 percent growth, upper 3.0 percent growth or above 4.0 percent growth."

"The manufacturing sector is also important," said Moran. "This is a cyclical area of the economy and it bears close watching. It looks like the average gain for the fourth quarter will be a solid one. There again we will see more exactly how strongly GDP grew in the fourth quarter."
Once the data is released and digested, however, the market should quiet down, participants said.
"I would guess that since the PSA (The Bond Market Trade Association) has recommended an early close, once we're past noon, things will get pretty quiet," said Moran.
The PSA recommended that trading in government securities end at 1400 EST/1900 GMT before the holiday weekend.
In early trade, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 3/32 to 95-28/32, yielding 6.82 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-19/32, yielding 5.97 percent. Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-6/32, yielding 6.32 percent. Ten-year notes were up 3/32 to 99-21/32, yielding 6.55 percent.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.03 percent. Six-month rates were up one basis point to 5.08 percent and year bill rates were unchanged at 5.30 percent.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
